div.head: A b s t r a c t -Real-time expert systems are embedded decision systems which must respond to changes in the environments within stringent timing constraints. A major problem impeding the use of rule-based expert systems in real-time environments
div.p: is the difficulty in predicting the response time of these rule-based sys tems.

In this paper, we tackle this problem with a fast, partially parallelizable response time analysis al gorithm for a class of EQL rule-based programs with constant assignments in the action parts of the rules.

div.head: I N T R O D U C T I O N
div.p: Given a program p, the response time analysis prob lem is to determine the maxima] response time of p. Although real-time systems have received their share of attention in recent years, few attempts have been made to formally address the response time analysis problem. This is due to the fact that the response time analysis problem is undecidable if the program variable have infinite domains, and is PSPACE-hard in the case where all the variables have finite domains [4]. Instead, a great deal of efforts have focused on im proving the speed of execution. There has been a lot of discussions on exploiting the parallelism and several parallel processing techniques have been proposed and applied to enhance the performance of rule-based sys tems. However, fast execution helps in meeting strin gent timing constraints, but fast execution alone does not guarantee the fulfillment of timing constraints.

The EQuational Logic (EQL) language is a simple language designed for real-time applications. It was introduced in [1] as a model-investigation language to develop techniques to obtain the response time of rule-based programs. Browne et al [1] and Mok [4] reported a set of analysis tools, based on state space graph checking, to determine the response times of EQL programs. In an a t t e m p t to reduce the time required for conducting the response time analysis, we have observed that there are sets, each of which is called a S p e c i a l Form, of syntactic and semantic constraint assertions such that the execution of a set of rules always terminates in bounded time if this set of rules satisfies a Special Form.

In this paper, we introduce one of the observed The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly explains the syntax and the seman tics of the EQuational Logic language. In Section 3, we present Special Form B and Algorithm_B. Finally, Section 4 concludes this paper.

div.head: THE EQL LANGUAGE
div.p: An EQL program, p, has a set of rules for updating a set of variables which denote the state of the physical system under control. Sensor readings are sampled periodically. Every time sensor readings are taken, the variables are recomputed iteratively by a number of rule firings until no further change in the variables can result from the firing of a rule. The EQL program is then said to have reached a fixed p o i n t .

The set of variables is called the state variable, which consists of two parts: the input variables and the non-input variables. For each rule r in p, r is a conditional statement of the form where m > 1 and the symbol '|' stands for AND. For each i, 1 < i < m, aj is a non-input variable which is assigned the value of the expression 6j if the rule r is fired. EC is a predicate on the program variables and is called the E n a b l i n g C o n d i t i o n . div.head: Response Time
div.p: The execution of the program p is a sequence of r e c o g n i z e -act cycles. During each cycle, a firable rule is selected to fire, p reaches a fixed point if none of its rules is firable. The execution of p terminates when p reaches a fixed point. The r e s p o n s e t i m e of p is measured in terms of the number of rule firings during the execution of p. A r e s p o n s e t i m e u p p e r b o u n d of p is an integer not less than the maximal number of rule firings that can possibly happen dur ing the execution of p. Let T p represent a response time upper bound of the program p.

div.head: T h e General Analysis Algorithm
div.p: In the next section, we will introduce an observed Spe cial Form. However, for any EQL program p, it is rarely the case that p as a whole is in a known Spe cial Form. Instead, it. is frequently found that p can be partitioned into a hierarchy of sets of rules such that some of these sets are in a known Special Form. In order to exploit this property and to enhance the applicability of the response time upper bound algo rithm presented later, the General Analysis Algorithm [2] is adopted to partition the given program into sub sets such that only a subset of the program is analyzed at a time. This strategy takes advantage of the fact that the given program has a bounded response time if and only if all of the subsets have bounded response times.

div.p: A S p e c i a l Forin is a set of syntactic and semantic constraint assertions such that if a set of rules satis fies all of these assertions, then the execution of this set of rules always terminates in bounded time. The Special Form introduced in this paper is called Special Form B. We will also present an algorithm, namely Algorithm_B, used to compute response time upper bounds of programs satisfying Special Form B. First of all, some definitions are in order.

div.p: We now present an algorithm used to com pute response time upper bounds of programs satisfying Special Form B. The strategy here is to partition the rule firings into two sets: rule firings made possible by the launch state and rule firings made possible by rule firings.

It has been found that there are sets of syntactic and semantic constraint assertions such that if p satisfies any of them, the exe cution of p always terminates in bounded time. Each of these sets of syntactic constraint assertions is called a Special Form. In this paper, the existence of a Special Form, namely Special Form B, has been proved. T h e most time-consuming part to recognize if a set of rule is in Special Form B is in the construction of the ME graph and the ER graph. We have shown how to parallelize these construction procedures. Algorithm_B, which takes advantage of the characteristics of the Special Form B, has been developed to obtain response time upper bounds for programs satisfying Special Form B.

By using the proposed approach, we have success fully reduced the time needed to analyze some real-life real-time rule-based systems. Currently, we are devel oping new algorithms exploiting the characteristics of Special Forms such that tighter response time upper bounds for EQL programs can be obtained. T h e de velopment of new Special Forms is also under way.
